subject: Coffee & Tea
title: First Crack and Second Crack
description: A micro-lesson that makes First Crack and Second Crack usable.

hook.text: During roasting, coffee beans literally crack—twice. Each crack signals a critical chemical milestone.

buildup.text: First crack happens around 196°C. Steam pressure inside the bean breaks the cell structure. It sounds like popcorn.

discovery.text: After first crack, origin flavors emerge: fruit, floral, citrus. This is where light roasts stop.

twist.text: Second crack occurs near 224°C as oils migrate to the surface. The bean darkens and smoky flavors dominate.

climax.text: Past second crack, roast flavors overpower origin. Dark roasts taste more like the roast than the bean.

punchline.text: Two cracks, two choices. Origin flavor or roast flavor.

quiz.question: What happens at first crack during coffee roasting?
options: Steam pressure breaks cell structure, releasing origin flavors

details.summary: During roasting, coffee beans audibly crack twice. First crack occurs around 196 degrees Celsius as moisture turns to steam and the bean expands. Second crack at about 224 degrees breaks down the cell structure itself. Most specialty coffees are roasted between these two markers.
details.whyItMatters: The cracks are the roaster's most important audio cues. They define the boundaries of roast development and directly influence flavor.
takeaways: First crack happens around 196 degrees Celsius
Second crack occurs near 224 degrees as cell walls fracture
Most specialty coffees are roasted between the two cracks

faq.question: What happens to flavor at each crack stage?
faq.answer: Before first crack, beans are grassy and undeveloped. After first crack, fruity and acidic notes emerge. Between cracks, sweetness and body peak. After second crack, smoky and bitter notes dominate as sugars carbonize and oils surface.

faq.question: Can you roast past second crack safely?
faq.answer: Yes, but carefully. Italian and French roasts push well past second crack. However, the beans become very oily and fragile, and there is a risk of fire in the roaster. Most roasters stay below or just into second crack for dark roasts.
